More than half of the benefit of the CGT concession went to the top 1% of income earners, the most recent data shows Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? Sign up for The Crunch here This year’s federal budget includes changes to negative gearing and capital gains (CGT) and discretionary trust tax concessions – policies that some blame for fuelling housing speculation and that disproportionately benefit the richest. The top 1% of lifetime earners alone have received more than $700,000 in tax concessions over their working life from capital gains tax, negative gearing and discretionary trusts, according to figures in the budget.

In 2022-23 – the most recent data – the top 10% of income earners received 83% of the benefit of the capital gains tax concession and 37% of negative gearing. The vast majority of the benefit of both went to people earning above the then median income of $58,216. Capital gains taxes are the tax paid on the profits (the “gains”) when you sell an asset – like a house – for a profit. Under changes introduced in 1999, investors get a 50% discount in capital gains tax if they hold on to the asset for more than a year. Negative gearing (what the Treasury calls “rental loss”) is when an investment property makes a loss – like if the rental income doesn’t pay the mortgage – and the losses are tax deductible against a landlord’s income.

Early speculation was that the CGT discount could reduce to 33%, but The Australian revealed on the weekend that the 50% capital gains tax discount would be axed in favour of inflation indexation on new ­investments across every asset class, but current investors would be protected by partial grandfathering, under a budget tax overhaul the Albanese government is close to finalising. If changes occur next month, investors will rethink how they own property assets. Currently, negative gearing favours high-income earners as it provides the ability to claim up to 47% of rental losses against the tax on employment income. Capital gains tax, on the other hand, favours low-income earners, given that gains are added to a person’s taxable income with a 50% discount in most cases.

[Lähde: The Guardian World]
More than half of the benefit of the CGT concession went to the top 1% of income earners, the most recent data shows

Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? Sign up for The Crunch here

This year’s federal budget includes changes to negative gearing and capital gains (CGT) and discretionary trust tax concessions – policies that some blame for fuelling housing speculation and that disproportionately benefit the richest.

The top 1% of lifetime earners alone have received more than $700,000 in tax concessions over their working life from capital gains tax, negative gearing and discretionary trusts, according to figures in the budget.

In 2022-23 – the most recent data – the top 10% of income earners received 83% of the benefit of the capital gains tax concession and 37% of negative gearing. The vast majority of the benefit of both went to people earning above the then median income of $58,216.

Capital gains taxes are the tax paid on the profits (the “gains”) when you sell an asset – like a house – for a profit. Under changes introduced in 1999, investors get a 50% discount in capital gains tax if they hold on to the asset for more than a year.

Negative gearing (what the Treasury calls “rental loss”) is when an investment property makes a loss – like if the rental income doesn’t pay the mortgage – and the losses are tax deductible against a landlord’s income.

The vast majority of both tax benefits went to those who earn above the median income.

Of the more than 1 million tax filers in 2022-23, just 71% actually benefited from the capital gains tax discount. Almost all of this – 95% – went to Australians earning above the median income.

But even among the better off, there is a huge inequality – more than half of the capital gains tax benefit went to the top 1% of income earners.

---

[Lähde: Stockhead]
The federal budget is set to change the landscape for property investors. Pic: Getty Images

Property investors have enjoyed a stable tax system regarding capital gains and negative gearing for more than a quarter of a century.

It’s been 27 years since the Howard government ditched the indexation method on capital gains and replaced it with a flat 50% discount for assets held over 12 months. But the upcoming May budget is likely to bring change, with the federal government foreshadowing a tightening of the rules.

Of the potential options Labor is considering, it may reinstate the 1985 Hawke-Keating system, where property losses are quarantined and can only offset future property income and capital gains; or adopt the ill-fated Bill Shorten proposal, which restricts negative gearing to brand-new properties.

Early speculation was that the CGT discount could reduce to 33%, but The Australian revealed on the weekend that the 50% capital gains tax discount would be axed in favour of inflation indexation on new ­investments across every asset class, but current investors would be protected by partial grandfathering, under a budget tax overhaul the Albanese government is close to finalising.

If changes occur next month, investors will rethink how they own property assets.

Currently, negative gearing favours high-income earners as it provides the ability to claim up to 47% of rental losses against the tax on employment income. Capital gains tax, on the other hand, favours low-income earners, given that gains are added to a person’s taxable income with a 50% discount in most cases.

If negative gearing is restricted and the CGT discount reduced, owning investment property in individual names will become distinctly less attractive, and people may turn to more complex structures.

The first port of call is usually a family trust; however, there may also be changes to this structure in the budget.

At present, family trusts are used as a “flow through” vehicle whereby the trustees, usually the parents, allocate the income and gains generated each year from the family trust to the beneficiaries, who then get taxed at their own marginal tax rate.

This works particularly well if there are low-income beneficiaries such as children at university with casual jobs.

But the tax flexibility of family trusts may also be under threat in the budget, with Treasury modelling potential changes to family trusts that would increase tax revenue by $3bn per year.

payload.title: Australian verotuet kasautuvat tuoreiden lukujen mukaan suurituloisille
payload.summary: Australian budjettilukujen mukaan luovutusvoittoveron alennus, negatiivinen velkavipu ja harkinnanvaraiset trustit hyödyttävät suhteettoman paljon kaikkein suurituloisimpia.
payload.content:
Australian tuoreimmat verotiedot osoittavat, että sijoittajille suunnatut veroedut kasautuvat vahvasti tulohaitarin yläpäähän. Vuoden 2022–2023 aineiston mukaan suurituloisin kymmenesosa sai 83 prosenttia luovutusvoittoveron alennuksen hyödystä ja 37 prosenttia negatiivisen velkavivun hyödystä. Budjettilukujen mukaan kaikkein suurituloisin yksi prosentti on saanut työuransa aikana yli 700 000 Australian dollarin arvosta veroetuja luovutusvoittoverosta, negatiivisesta velkavivusta ja harkinnanvaraisista trusteista.

## Hyödyt painottuvat mediaanitulon yläpuolelle

Tuoreiden tietojen mukaan sekä luovutusvoittoveron alennuksen että negatiivisen velkavivun hyödyt menevät valtaosin ihmisille, joiden tulot ylittävät silloisen mediaanitulon, 58 216 Australian dollaria. Tämä tekee järjestelmistä poliittisesti kiistanalaisia, koska niitä on arvosteltu varakkaimpien kotitalouksien suosimisesta.

Luovutusvoittoveroa maksetaan voitosta, joka syntyy esimerkiksi asunnon tai muun omaisuuserän myynnistä. Australiassa vuonna 1999 käyttöön otettujen sääntöjen mukaan sijoittaja voi saada 50 prosentin alennuksen luovutusvoittoverosta, jos omaisuutta on pidetty yli vuoden ajan. Negatiivinen velkavipu taas tarkoittaa tilannetta, jossa sijoitusasunto tuottaa tappiota esimerkiksi siksi, että vuokratulot eivät kata lainakuluja. Tappio voidaan vähentää vuokranantajan muista tuloista verotuksessa.

## Budjetissa arvioidaan muutoksia verohuojennuksiin

Veroedut ovat nousseet esiin Australian liittovaltion budjettikeskustelussa. Budjetissa käsitellään muutoksia negatiiviseen velkavipuun, luovutusvoittoveroon ja harkinnanvaraisiin trusteihin. Näitä käytäntöjä on arvosteltu siitä, että ne voivat ruokkia asuntospekulaatiota ja ohjata suurimmat hyödyt eniten ansaitseville.

Keskustelussa on ollut esillä luovutusvoittoveron alennuksen muuttaminen. Varhaisissa arvioissa puhuttiin alennuksen laskemisesta 33 prosenttiin, mutta myöhemmin esillä on ollut malli, jossa nykyinen 50 prosentin alennus korvattaisiin uusissa sijoituksissa inflaatioindeksillä. Nykyisiä sijoittajia saatettaisiin suojata osittaisilla siirtymäsäännöillä.

Mahdolliset muutokset vaikuttaisivat siihen, miten sijoittajat omistavat asuntoja ja muuta omaisuutta. Negatiivinen velkavipu on erityisen arvokas suurituloisille, koska se voi antaa mahdollisuuden vähentää jopa 47 prosenttia vuokratappioista palkkatulojen verotuksessa. Siksi budjettiratkaisuissa on kyse myös siitä, kenelle verojärjestelmän suurimmat huojennukset lopulta kohdistuvat.

Veroedut ovat nousseet esiin Australian liittovaltion budjettikeskustelussa. Budjetissa käsitellään muutoksia negatiiviseen velkavipuun, luovutusvoittoveroon ja harkinnanvaraisiin trusteihin. Näitä käytäntöjä on arvosteltu siitä, että ne voivat ruokkia asuntospekulaatiota ja ohjata suurimmat hyödyt eniten ansaitseville.

Keskustelussa on ollut esillä luovutusvoittoveron alennuksen muuttaminen. Varhaisissa arvioissa puhuttiin alennuksen laskemisesta 33 prosenttiin, mutta myöhemmin esillä on ollut malli, jossa nykyinen 50 prosentin alennus korvattaisiin uusissa sijoituksissa inflaatioindeksillä. Nykyisiä sijoittajia saatettaisiin suojata osittaisilla siirtymäsäännöillä.

Mahdolliset muutokset vaikuttaisivat siihen, miten sijoittajat omistavat asuntoja ja muuta omaisuutta. Negatiivinen velkavipu on erityisen arvokas suurituloisille, koska se voi antaa mahdollisuuden vähentää jopa 47 prosenttia vuokratappioista palkkatulojen verotuksessa. Siksi budjettiratkaisuissa on kyse myös siitä, kenelle verojärjestelmän suurimmat huojennukset lopulta kohdistuvat.

Sign up for The Crunch here This year’s federal budget includes changes to negative gearing and capital gains (CGT) and discretionary trust tax concessions – policies that some blame for fuelling housing speculation and that disproportionately benefit the richest. The top 1% of lifetime earners alone have received more than $700,000 in tax concessions over their working life from capital gains tax, negative gearing and discretionary trusts, according to figures in the budget.

In 2022-23 – the most recent data – the top 10% of income earners received 83% of the benefit of the capital gains tax concession and 37% of negative gearing. The vast majority of the benefit of both went to people earning above the then median income of $58,216. Capital gains taxes are the tax paid on the profits (the “gains”) when you sell an asset – like a house – for a profit. Under changes introduced in 1999, investors get a 50% discount in capital gains tax if they hold on to the asset for more than a year. Negative gearing (what the Treasury calls “rental loss”) is when an investment property makes a loss – like if the rental income doesn’t pay the mortgage – and the losses are tax deductible against a landlord’s income.

Early speculation was that the CGT discount could reduce to 33%, but The Australian revealed on the weekend that the 50% capital gains tax discount would be axed in favour of inflation indexation on new ­investments across every asset class, but current investors would be protected by partial grandfathering, under a budget tax overhaul the Albanese government is close to finalising. If changes occur next month, investors will rethink how they own property assets. Currently, negative gearing favours high-income earners as it provides the ability to claim up to 47% of rental losses against the tax on employment income. Capital gains tax, on the other hand, favours low-income earners, given that gains are added to a person’s taxable income with a 50% discount in most cases.
